paragraphs.text: A rolled [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) from 1980, kept for forty-six years in the island's tradition of [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea. Leaf chosen for keeping starts out well roasted and dry. It is roasted again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in, and kept cool, dark and sealed between roastings. No standard says when an oolong becomes old. Those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty years, and this tea is sixteen years past the longest of them.

The label names only [Taiwan](taiwan:on-a-label). That places the leaf on the island and says nothing more: no mountain, no township, no cultivar. What it does carry is the island's own craft. [Oolong](oolong:definition) is the partly oxidised tea between green and red, and the island's trade is built on [rolled, bead-shaped oolong](taiwan:known-for) like this one.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
